claim: Dengue virus (DENV) causes approximately 400 million infections in humans each year.
source: Dengue virus (DENV) is the most significant human arboviral pathogen and causes ∼400 million infections in humans each year.
evidence: This is stated as a factual assertion in the abstract without supporting data in the manuscript, but is presented as established knowledge about DENV epidemiology.

claim: Mast cells mediate vascular leakage during DENV infection in mice.
source: In previous work, we observed that mast cells (MC) mediate vascular leakage during DENV infection in mice and that levels of MC activation are correlated with disease severity in human DENV patients (St John et al., 2013b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work by the authors.

claim: Levels of mast cell activation are correlated with disease severity in human DENV patients.
source: In previous work, we observed that mast cells (MC) mediate vascular leakage during DENV infection in mice and that levels of MC activation are correlated with disease severity in human DENV patients (St John et al., 2013b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: A major risk factor for developing severe dengue is secondary infection with a heterologous serotype.
source: A major risk factor for developing severe dengue is secondary infection with a heterologous serotype.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge in the field of dengue research.

claim: Cross-reactive but non-neutralizing antibodies promote uptake of virus and allow enhanced replication during secondary DENV infection.
source: The dominant theory explaining increased severity during secondary DENV infection is that cross-reactive but non-neutralizing antibodies promote uptake of virus and allow enhanced replication.
evidence: This is presented as the dominant theory in the field, representing established knowledge.

claim: FcγR-mediated enhanced degranulation responses by mast cells contribute to enhanced vascular leakage during secondary DENV infection.
source: Here, we define another mechanism, dependent on FcγR-mediated enhanced degranulation responses by MCs.
evidence: This is the primary claim of the manuscript, supported by experimental data presented throughout the results section.

claim: Antibody-dependent mast cell activation constitutes a novel mechanism to explain enhanced vascular leakage during secondary DENV infection.
source: Antibody-dependent mast cell activation constitutes a novel mechanism to explain enhanced vascular leakage during secondary DENV infection.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the experimental data presented.

claim: Dengue hemorrhagic fever (DHF) and dengue shock syndrome (DSS) are characterized by increased vascular permeability and plasma leakage into tissues.
source: More severe forms of the disease include dengue hemorrhagic fever (DHF) and dengue shock syndrome (DSS), which are characterized by increased vascular permeability and plasma leakage into tissues (Halstead, 2007; St John et al., 2013a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: There are four major serotypes of DENV that infect humans.
source: There are four major serotypes of DENV that infect humans, and a primary DENV infection with any of the four serotypes elicits long-lived antibodies against the primary infection serotype (St John et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is established knowledge in dengue virology.

claim: A primary DENV infection elicits long-lived antibodies against the primary infection serotype.
source: There are four major serotypes of DENV that infect humans, and a primary DENV infection with any of the four serotypes elicits long-lived antibodies against the primary infection serotype (St John et al., 2013a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The DENV-specific humoral response is capable of preventing infection by neutralizing virus of the infecting serotype only.
source: Importantly, this DENV-specific humoral response is capable of preventing infection by neutralizing virus of the infecting serotype only.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about DENV immunity.

claim: Antibody responses generated during a primary DENV infection frequently show cross-reactivity to other DENV serotypes but are largely non-neutralizing.
source: Although the antibody response generated during a primary infection frequently shows some cross-reactivity to other DENV serotypes, these responses are largely non-neutralizing towards viruses of other DENV serotypes (Halstead, 2007; Rothman, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Symptomatic re-infection with the same DENV serotype experienced during primary infection has never been reported.
source: Symptomatic re-infection with the same serotype that had been experienced during primary infection has never been reported; therefore, immunological memory is understood to be highly effective against a secondary infection with a homologous serotype (Sabin, 1952).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Immunological memory is highly effective against a secondary infection with a homologous DENV serotype.
source: Symptomatic re-infection with the same serotype that had been experienced during primary infection has never been reported; therefore, immunological memory is understood to be highly effective against a secondary infection with a homologous serotype (Sabin, 1952).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that symptomatic re-infection with the same serotype has never been reported, supported by citation.

claim: Symptomatic secondary infection with a heterologous DENV serotype is relatively common in DENV-endemic regions.
source: In contrast, symptomatic secondary infection with a heterologous serotype of DENV is relatively common in DENV-endemic regions (Low et al., 2006; Guilarde et al., 2008; Anderson et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior epidemiological studies.

claim: There is an increased risk of developing DHF due to a secondary infection with a heterologous DENV serotype.
source: Some studies have shown that there is an increased risk of developing DHF due to a secondary infection with a heterologous DENV serotype, or as a result of the presence of maternally transferred heterologous antibodies (Halstead et al., 1970; Halstead, 1988; Kliks et al., 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Presence of maternally transferred heterologous antibodies increases the risk of developing DHF.
source: Some studies have shown that there is an increased risk of developing DHF due to a secondary infection with a heterologous DENV serotype, or as a result of the presence of maternally transferred heterologous antibodies (Halstead et al., 1970; Halstead, 1988; Kliks et al., 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: More severe DENV infections are associated with higher levels of virus replication.
source: It is thought that more severe infections are associated with higher levels of virus replication, which could be attributed to cellular uptake of immune complexes that are internalized by immunoglobulin Fc-receptor (FcR) bearing cells, such as dendritic cells and macrophages (Kliks et al., 1988).
evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis in the field, supported by citation.

claim: ADE-promoting immune complexes are generated when pre-existing, non-neutralizing antibodies cross-react with an antigenically distinct heterologous DENV serotype.
source: ADE-promoting immune complexes are generated when pre-existing, non-neutralizing antibodies cross-react with an antigenically distinct heterologous DENV serotype.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about the ADE mechanism.

claim: Increased viral infection as a result of ADE leads to increased secretion of vasoactive immune products by infected cells.
source: It is thought that increased viral infection as a result of ADE leads to increased secretion of vasoactive immune products by infected cells, such as TNF-α, which may promote vascular leakage during DHF (Kliks et al., 1988).
evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis in the field, supported by citation.

claim: Conflicting information exists regarding the association of TNF-α with severe dengue.
source: Conflicting information regarding the association of TNF-α, specifically, with severe dengue has been reported (Hober et al., 1993; Chakravarti and Kumaria, 2006) but cytokines produced by DENV-infected cells remain the leading suspects for inducing severe dengue (St John et al., 2013a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies showing conflicting results.

claim: Cytokines produced by DENV-infected cells remain the leading suspects for inducing severe dengue.
source: Conflicting information regarding the association of TNF-α, specifically, with severe dengue has been reported (Hober et al., 1993; Chakravarti and Kumaria, 2006) but cytokines produced by DENV-infected cells remain the leading suspects for inducing severe dengue (St John et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is presented as the current consensus in the field, supported by citation.

claim: ADE alone is not sufficient to explain the vascular pathology associated with DHF since many individuals experience DHF during primary infection.
source: Although ADE, alone, is not sufficient to explain the vascular pathology associated with DHF since many individuals also experience DHF during primary infection, it can explain antibody-dependent increases in viral uptake and infection burden that could promote downstream pathogenesis (St John et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is a logical inference based on clinical observations, supported by citation.

claim: Weakly neutralizing antibodies against DENV structural proteins have been observed in human DENV patients.
source: Weakly neutralizing antibodies against the DENV structural proteins, including envelope (E) protein domain III and precursor membrane protein, have been observed in human DENV patients (Dejnirattisai et al., 2010; Wahala et al., 2012) and the phenomenon of ADE has been shown in vitro and in animal models (Halstead et al., 1973; Shresta et al., 2006); however, ADE has not yet been observed in human DENV patients (St John et al., 2013a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The phenomenon of ADE has been shown in vitro and in animal models.
source: Weakly neutralizing antibodies against the DENV structural proteins, including envelope (E) protein domain III and precursor membrane protein, have been observed in human DENV patients (Dejnirattisai et al., 2010; Wahala et al., 2012) and the phenomenon of ADE has been shown in vitro and in animal models (Halstead et al., 1973; Shresta et al., 2006); however, ADE has not yet been observed in human DENV patients (St John et al., 2013a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: ADE has not yet been observed in human DENV patients.
source: Weakly neutralizing antibodies against the DENV structural proteins, including envelope (E) protein domain III and precursor membrane protein, have been observed in human DENV patients (Dejnirattisai et al., 2010; Wahala et al., 2012) and the phenomenon of ADE has been shown in vitro and in animal models (Halstead et al., 1973; Shresta et al., 2006); however, ADE has not yet been observed in human DENV patients (St John et al., 2013a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Mast cells express a wide range of Fc receptors.
source: Mast cells (MCs), for example, are granulated cells that express a wide range of Fc receptors (Abraham and St John, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Mast cells can bind multiple classes of antibodies, including IgE and IgG.
source: This allows them to bind multiple classes of antibodies, including IgE (through FcεRI) and IgG (through FcγRs) (Sylvestre and Ravetch, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Human mast cells express the inhibitory IgG receptor FcγRIIb and the activating receptors FcγRI and FcγRIIa.
source: Human MCs have been shown to express the inhibitory IgG receptor, FcγRIIb, as well as the activating receptors, FcγRI and FcγRIIa (which are functionally analogous to FcγRIII on mice), albeit with some variations based on tissue and cell activation state (Sylvestre and Ravetch, 1996; Okayama et al., 2000; Malbec and Daëron, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Mast cells are important for pathogen immunosurveillance and pre-store many vasoactive mediators within their granules.
source: MCs are important for pathogen immunosurveillance and pre-store many vasoactive mediators within their granules (Abraham and St John, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Mast cells are localized in tissues near the vasculature.
source: Recent reports showed that MCs, which are localized in tissues near the vasculature (Kunder et al., 2011), are directly activated by DENV, resulting in the release of their pre-formed mediators through the process of degranulation (St John et al., 2011, 2013b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Mast cells are directly activated by DENV, resulting in the release of their pre-formed mediators through degranulation.
source: Recent reports showed that MCs, which are localized in tissues near the vasculature (Kunder et al., 2011), are directly activated by DENV, resulting in the release of their pre-formed mediators through the process of degranulation (St John et al., 2011, 2013b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claim: DENV-elicited mast cell vasoactive products enhance vascular leakage in animal models.
source: In our previous study, we showed that DENV-elicited MC vasoactive products enhance vascular leakage in animal models (St John et al., 2013b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: DHF patients with secondary infection display higher serum levels of the mast cell-derived protein chymase compared to DHF patients with primary infection.
source: We also reported that DHF patients with secondary infection, in contrast to DHF patients with primary infection, displayed higher serum levels of the MC-derived protein chymase, a biomarker that is specifically produced by MCs and associated with MC activation (St John et al., 2013b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Chymase is a biomarker specifically produced by mast cells and associated with mast cell activation.
source: We also reported that DHF patients with secondary infection, in contrast to DHF patients with primary infection, displayed higher serum levels of the MC-derived protein chymase, a biomarker that is specifically produced by MCs and associated with MC activation (St John et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge, supported by citation.

claim: Mast cell degranulation levels are higher in patients with secondary DENV infection.
source: We also reported that DHF patients with secondary infection, in contrast to DHF patients with primary infection, displayed higher serum levels of the MC-derived protein chymase, a biomarker that is specifically produced by MCs and associated with MC activation (St John et al., 2013b). This suggests that MC degranulation levels are higher in patients with secondary infection, raising the question of how MC responses could be enhanced, mechanistically, during secondary infection (St John, 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of higher chymase levels in secondary infection patients.

claim: IgG is efficiently bound by Fc-receptor bearing cells when antibody and antigen aggregate in immune complexes.
source: IgG is efficiently bound by Fc-receptor bearing cells when antibody and antigen aggregate in immune complexes.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge in immunology.

claim: Mast cells can be infected through ADE when immune complexes containing non-neutralized DENV are taken up via Fc receptor-mediated endocytosis.
source: Similarly to other Fc-receptor bearing cells, MCs also can be infected through the process of ADE when immune complexes containing non-neutralized DENV are taken up via Fc receptor-mediated endocytosis (King et al., 2000; Goncalvez et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Mast cells can become sensitized by pre-existing circulating antibodies through binding to Fc receptors.
source: However, in addition to endocytosis of immune complexes, MCs act as effectors of the adaptive immune system due to their ability to become sensitized by pre-existing circulating antibodies through binding to the Fc receptors (Abraham and St John, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Affinity for IgG receptors increases substantially when antibody is bound in immune complexes.
source: When antibody is bound in immune complexes, affinity for the IgG receptors increases substantially (Takizawa et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Antibody-sensitized mast cells can become activated when the sensitizing-antigen binds to Ig and cross-links the FcRs.
source: Antibody-sensitized MCs can become activated during a secondary challenge when the sensitizing-antigen binds to Ig and cross-links the FcRs or can be activated through binding of immune complexes that have already been formed (Oshiba et al., 1996; Malbec and Daëron, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Mast cells sensitized with post-immune serum containing IgE antibodies have increased degranulation in response to DENV in vitro.
source: In vitro, it has been shown that MCs sensitized with post-immune serum containing IgE antibodies have increased degranulation in response to DENV (Sanchez et al., 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Increased DENV-specific IgE antibody levels have been associated with DHF.
source: Interestingly, increased DENV-specific IgE antibody levels have been associated with DHF (Koraka et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: IgG immune complexes can promote mast cell degranulation in mice.
source: With regards to IgG-mediated MC activation, studies have also shown that IgG immune complexes can promote MC degranulation in mice (Vaz and Ovary, 1968; Vaz and Prouvost-Danon, 1969; Daëron et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Mice deficient in FcγRIII lack IgG-mediated mast cell degranulation.
source: Moreover, mice deficient in FcγRIII lack IgG-mediated MC degranulation, have an impaired Arthus reaction, and are resistant to IgG-dependent passive anaphylaxis (Hazenbos et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Mice deficient in FcγRIII have an impaired Arthus reaction.
source: Moreover, mice deficient in FcγRIII lack IgG-mediated MC degranulation, have an impaired Arthus reaction, and are resistant to IgG-dependent passive anaphylaxis (Hazenbos et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Mice deficient in FcγRIII are resistant to IgG-dependent passive anaphylaxis.
source: Moreover, mice deficient in FcγRIII lack IgG-mediated MC degranulation, have an impaired Arthus reaction, and are resistant to IgG-dependent passive anaphylaxis (Hazenbos et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Sensitization of mast cells with 4G2 antibody significantly increases the magnitude of mast cell degranulation in response to DENV2 compared to virus exposure alone.
source: However, we found that sensitization of MCs with 4G2 significantly increases the magnitude of MC degranulation in response to DENV2, compared to virus exposure alone (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Increasing concentrations of 4G2 antibody result in incrementally increased mast cell degranulation in a dose-dependent fashion.
source: Furthermore, increasing concentrations of antibody resulted in incrementally increased MC degranulation in a dose-dependent fashion (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Pre-treatment with anti-E antibody 4G2 significantly enhances mast cell degranulation in vivo over the levels induced by DENV exposure alone.
source: Both techniques revealed that MC degranulation occurs in response to DENV alone (as previously reported [St John et al., 2011]) but that pre-treatment with the anti-E antibody 4G2 significantly enhances MC-degranulation in vivo over the levels induced by DENV exposure alone (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1B and 1C.

claim: DENV-specific IgG antibodies have the potential to enhance mast cell responses in vivo.
source: These data show that DENV-specific IgG antibodies have the potential to enhance MC responses in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: DENV-induced mast cell degranulation increases endothelial permeability in vitro and vascular leakage in vivo during primary infection of naïve animals.
source: We have previously reported that DENV-induced MC degranulation increases endothelial permeability in vitro, and vascular leakage in vivo during primary infection of naïve animals (St John et al., 2013b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Mice pre-sensitized with 4G2 antibody prior to DENV2 infection had significantly increased hematocrit values compared to those infected with DENV in the absence of antibody.
source: Measurement of hematocrit levels at 24 hr and 48 hr post-DENV2 infection showed that mice that had been pre-sensitized to DENV by injection with 4G2 antibody prior to DENV2 infection had significantly increased hematocrit values compared to those that were infected with DENV in the absence of the antibody (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Hematocrit values were increased in antibody pre-treated mice, but virus levels were not significantly increased in the spleen at 24 hr post-infection.
source: Interestingly, although the hematocrit values were increased in antibody pre-treated mice, the levels of virus were not significantly increased in the spleen (St John et al., 2013b), a DENV-target organ, (Figure 1E) at the same time point.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The cross-reactive antibody 4G2 enhances mast cell degranulation in response to all four serotypes of DENV.
source: By β-hexosaminidase assay, we observed increased degranulation in the presence of the 4G2 antibody for all four serotypes of DENV, compared to DENV treatment alone (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The DENV2-specific 3H5 antibody only enhances DENV2-induced degranulation but does not significantly change degranulation levels induced by DENV1, 3, or 4.
source: In contrast, the DENV2-specific 3H5 antibody only enhanced DENV2-induced degranulation over DENV2 alone treatment, but did not significantly change the levels of degranulation induced by MC exposure to DENV1, 3, or 4 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Specificity or cross-reactivity of antibody for the infecting DENV serotype is required for antibody-mediated enhanced mast cell degranulation in vitro.
source: Therefore, specificity or cross-reactivity of antibody for the infecting DENV serotype is required for antibody-mediated enhanced MC degranulation in vitro.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figures 2A and 2B.

claim: Mice pre-sensitized with 4G2 prior to DENV1 infection had higher hematocrit values compared to those sensitized with control antibody.
source: We found that mice pre-sensitized with 4G2 prior to DENV1 infection had higher hematocrit values compared to those sensitized with control antibody, while 3H5 produced no enhancing effect during DENV1 infection (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The DENV2-specific antibody 3H5 produced no enhancing effect on hematocrit during DENV1 infection.
source: We found that mice pre-sensitized with 4G2 prior to DENV1 infection had higher hematocrit values compared to those sensitized with control antibody, while 3H5 produced no enhancing effect during DENV1 infection (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: DENV1 infection alone increased vascular leakage over control values, but leakage was significantly enhanced in the presence of antibody 4G2.
source: Using this technique as a secondary method to assess vascular leakage quantitatively, we observed that while DENV1 alone increased vascular leakage over control values, the leakage was significantly enhanced in the presence of antibody 4G2 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: DENV2-specific 3H5 antibody had no effect on vascular leakage when administered prior to a DENV1 challenge.
source: Again, in contrast to the DENV1–4 cross-reactive antibody 4G2, DENV2-specific 3H5 had no effect on vascular leakage when administered prior to a DENV1 challenge (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Enhanced vascular leakage DENV induces in the presence of antibodies is dependent on antibody specificity to the infecting DENV-serotype.
source: These findings support that the enhanced vascular leakage DENV induces in the presence of antibodies is dependent on antibody specificity to the infecting DENV-serotype.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 2.

claim: WT mice had substantially higher hematocrit values during DENV2 infection in the presence of DENV2-specific antibodies, while MC-deficient Sash mice showed no changes in hematocrit over baseline controls.
source: Hematocrit analysis supported MC-dependent antibody-enhanced vascular leakage since WT mice had substantially higher hematocrit values during DENV2 infection in the presence of DENV2-specific antibodies, while MC-deficient Sash mice showed no changes in hematocrit over baseline controls for either DENV2 treatment alone or treatment with 3H5 and DENV2 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Mast cells are required for increased DENV-induced, antibody-enhanced vascular permeability.
source: This observation that MCs are required for increased DENV-induced, antibody-enhanced vascular permeability, although qualitative in Figure 3B, was consistent with the significantly increased vascular leakage in the presence of antibody that was quantitated in Figure 3A.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: Cromolyn treatment successfully reduced both DENV-induced vascular leakage alone and antibody-enhanced DENV vascular leakage.
source: Cromolyn treatment successfully reduced both DENV-induced vascular leakage, alone, as well as antibody-enhanced DENV vascular leakage (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Antibody-enhanced response was abrogated by FcγRIII deficiency in BMMCs exposed to DENV2 with 4G2 or 3H5 antibodies.
source: BMMC degranulation responses to DENV were significantly enhanced in WT BMMCs pre-treated with either antibody, while the antibody-enhanced response was abrogated by FcγRIII deficiency (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: No difference was observed for direct degranulation responses to DENV in FcγRIII-KO BMMCs compared to WT BMMCs.
source: No difference was observed for direct degranulation responses to DENV in FcγRIII-KO BMMCs compared to WT BMMCs (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Only 4G2, and not 3H5, enhanced WT BMMC degranulation responses to DENV1, but this 4G2-dependent enhancement was not observed in FcγRIII-KO BMMCs.
source: As expected, only 4G2, and not 3H5, enhanced WT BMMC degranulation responses to DENV1, but this 4G2-dependent enhancement was not observed in FcγRIII-KO BMMCs (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Mast cell degranulation occurs independent of DENV replication.
source: We have previously shown that MC degranulation occurs independent of DENV replication (St John et al., 2011), and consistent results were obtained in this study, where there was not a significant difference between degranulation of BMMCs exposed to DENV or UV-inactivated DENV (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work and experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The DENV-specific antibody 4G2 enhanced degranulation of WT BMMCs to a similar extent when exposed to either DENV or UV-inactivated DENV.
source: The DENV-specific antibody 4G2 also enhanced degranulation of WT BMMCs to a similar extent when exposed to either DENV or UV-inactivated DENV in the presence of 4G2 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: FcγRIII-KO BMMCs showed baseline degranulation responses but no enhanced degranulation in the presence of specific antibody.
source: In contrast, FcγRIII-KO BMMCs, showed baseline degranulation responses, but no enhanced degranulation in the presence of specific antibody (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Both antibody-treated groups of WT and FcγRIII-KO BMMCs had heightened levels of DENV NS1 compared to control cells.
source: Our results showed that both antibody-treated groups of WT, and FcγRIII-KO BMMCs had heightened levels of DENV NS1 compared to control cells, although 4G2-treated FcγRIII-KO BMMCs had reduced levels of DENV NS1 compared to 4G2-treated WT BMMCs (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: FcγRIII can contribute to ADE in BMMCs but is likely not the only Fc receptor responsible for enhanced replication observed in antibody-treated MCs.
source: These results demonstrate that FcγRIII can also contribute to ADE in BMMCs, but is likely not the only Fc receptor responsible for the enhanced replication that is observed in antibody-treated MCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 4F.

claim: FcγRIII-deficiency reduces the magnitude of ADE in mast cells but enhanced viral replication is not completely abrogated, while the antibody-dependent portion of the degranulation response is abrogated.
source: Furthermore, FcγRIII-deficiency reduces the magnitude of ADE in MCs but enhanced viral replication is not completely abrogated, while the antibody-dependent portion of the degranulation response is.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figures 4A-F.

claim: Sash mice repleted with WT BMMCs displayed higher hematocrit levels and EBD leakage into the liver in response to DENV2 infection after 4G2 sensitization, compared to mice reconstituted with FcγRIII-KO BMMCs.
source: In support of a role for MC-expressed FcγRIII in vascular leakage, Sash mice repleted WT BMMCs displayed higher hematocrit levels (Figure 4H) and EBD leakage into the liver (Figure 4I) in response to DENV2 infection after 4G2 sensitization, compared to mice reconstituted with FcγRIII-KO BMMCs in response to DENV2 infection after 4G2 sensitization.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4H and 4I.

claim: FcγRIII on mast cells plays an essential role in the antibody-enhanced vascular leakage during DENV infection.
source: These findings suggest that FcγRIII on MCs plays an essential role in the antibody-enhanced vascular leakage during DENV infection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figures 4G-I.

claim: The viral burden in the spleen 24 hr post-infection was not significantly different between mice that received control serum vs mice that received heterologous post-immune serum.
source: The viral burden in the spleen, assessed by real time RT-PCR, 24 hr post-infection, was not found to be significantly different between mice that received control serum vs mice that received heterologous post-immune serum (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Challenge with either DENV1 (heterologous) or DENV2 (homologous) enhanced vascular leakage in mice that had been adoptively transferred DENV2 post-immune serum, compared to mice adoptively transferred naïve serum.
source: When the vascular leakage of infected mice was measured by hematocrit 24 hr post-infection, we observed that i.p. challenge with either DENV1 (a heterologous challenge) or DENV2 (a homologous challenge) enhanced vascular leakage in mice that had been adoptively transferred DENV2 post-immune serum, compared to mice adoptively transferred naïve serum (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Elevated levels of MCPT1 could be detected in the serum of animals after both live and inactivated virus challenges.
source: Concurrently, elevated levels of MCPT1, which is a biomarker for MC activation, could be detected in the serum of animals after both live and inactivated virus challenges (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Mice pre-treated with 4G2 had significantly higher serum levels of MCPT1 than mice given live or UV-DENV challenges alone.
source: Mice pre-treated with 4G2 had significantly higher serum levels of MCPT1 than mice given the live or UV-DENV challenges alone (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Mice that were challenged with pOVA antigen alone did not have elevated hematocrit values at 24 hr, but mice that had been adoptively transferred OVA post-immune serum showed increased hematocrit values.
source: As expected, mice that were challenged with the pOVA antigen alone did not have elevated hematocrit values at 24 hr, but mice that had been adoptively transferred OVA post-immune serum showed increased hematocrit values (Figure 5F), supporting that vascular leakage was increased in these animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: FcγRIII on mast cells promotes increased vascular leakage during a secondary DENV challenge after post-immune serum transfer.
source: Similar to our findings after adoptive transfer of monoclonal antibodies (Figure 4G–I), FcγRIII on MC promoted increased vascular leakage during a secondary DENV challenge after post-immune serum transfer, since mice reconstituted with WT BMMCs had greatly enhanced vascular leakage responses over FcγRIII-KO BMMC-reconstituted mice (Figure 5H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: FcγRIII on mast cells is critical for the enhanced vascular leakage observed after a heterologous DENV challenge.
source: Our results support that FcγRIII on MCs is critical for the enhanced vascular leakage observed after a heterologous DENV challenge.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 5.

claim: DENV-induced mast cell degranulation during primary DENV infection results in the release of numerous mast cell products that can act on the vascular endothelium and influence the coagulation cascade.
source: We previously reported that DENV-induced MC degranulation during primary DENV infection results in the release of numerous MC products that can act on the vascular endothelium and influence the coagulation cascade (St John, 2013; St John et al., 2013b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claim: Mast cell granule-associated mediators include heparin, mast cell-specific proteases, cytokines such as TNF, and other vasoactive factors.
source: Some of these products include the anti-coagulant heparin, MC-specific proteases, cytokines such as TNF, and other vasoactive factors.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about mast cell products.

claim: Mast cell activation is already elevated in primary DHF patients over control or DF patients.
source: We previously detected the MC-specific product chymase at higher levels in the serum of DHF patients with secondary infection, compared to DHF patients experiencing primary infection (St John et al., 2013b). This suggested that MC activation (which is already elevated in primary DHF patients over control or DF patients [St John et al., 2013b]) is further heightened during secondary infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Pre-existing IgG is able to enhance both mast cell degranulation and mast cell-dependent vascular leakage during DENV infection.
source: In our current study, our data reveal that pre-existing IgG is able to enhance both MC degranulation and MC-dependent vascular leakage during DENV infection.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data throughout the results section.

claim: Mast cells have equivalent degranulation responses to live and inactivated virus.
source: We also found that MCs have equivalent degranulation responses to live and inactivated virus and that antibodies further enhance degranulation to live and inactivated virus similarly.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the results section.

claim: Antibodies further enhance degranulation to live and inactivated virus similarly.
source: We also found that MCs have equivalent degranulation responses to live and inactivated virus and that antibodies further enhance degranulation to live and inactivated virus similarly.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the results section.

claim: Mast cell activation can be augmented by DENV-specific IgG, constituting a novel second mechanism of antibody-enhanced immune pathology during DENV infection that is dependent on FcγR-mediated augmented mast cell degranulation responses.
source: The observation that MC activation can be augmented by DENV-specific IgG constitutes a novel second mechanism of antibody-enhanced immune pathology during DENV infection that is dependent not on enhanced virus replication but on FcγR-mediated augmented MC degranulation responses.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by experimental data throughout.

claim: Enhanced mast cell degranulation and mast cell-promoted vascular leakage relied on the ability of pre-existing antibody to bind to DENV.
source: Enhanced MC degranulation and MC-promoted vascular leakage in our system relied on the ability of pre-existing antibody to bind to DENV, since we saw that heterologous and homologous antibodies could enhance MC degranulation, but non-binding antibody (e.g., 3H5 which does not bind to DENV1) could not enhance degranulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the results section.

claim: Increased vascular leakage in response to experimentally established systemic infection was not observed in Sash mice, which lack mast cells.
source: Increased vascular leakage in response to experimentally established systemic infection was not observed in Sash mice, which lack MCs, demonstrating that the enhanced vascular leakage was MC dependent.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the results section.

claim: The mechanism of IgG-enhanced mast cell responses is dependent on mast cell-expressed FcγRIII.
source: Furthermore, serum-adoptive transfer studies demonstrate that the mechanism of IgG-enhanced MC responses is dependent on MC-expressed FcγRIII.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the results section.

claim: FcγRIII-deficiency had no effect on direct mast cell degranulation responses to DENV, and only affected the antibody-enhanced component of the degranulation response.
source: Importantly, FcγRIII-deficiency had no effect on direct MC degranulation responses to DENV, and only affected the antibody-enhanced component of the degranulation response.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the results section.

claim: Reconstitution of Sash mice with WT, FcγRIII-expressing mast cells promoted enhanced vascular leakage in vivo after either monoclonal antibody administration or adoptive transfer of post-immune serum.
source: Reconstitution of Sash mice with WT, FcγRIII-expressing MCs promoted enhanced vascular leakage in vivo after either monoclonal antibody administration or adoptive transfer of post-immune serum, while vascular leakage in mice reconstituted with FcγRIII-KO MCs did not reach the same heightened levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the results section.

claim: Homologous antibodies can also promote classical ADE responses involving enhanced replication.
source: Interestingly, even homologous serum could enhance MC-dependent vascular leakage in our system, where a sufficient dose of virus is injected i.p. to establish a systemic infection. Others have also observed that homologous antibodies can also promote classical ADE responses involving enhanced replication (Kliks et al., 1988; Yamanaka et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Homologous secondary DENV infections have never been reported in humans and are assumed to be quickly cleared due to a strong and neutralizing adaptive immune response, without the development of symptoms.
source: However, homologous secondary DENV infections have never been reported in humans and are assumed to be quickly cleared due to a strong and neutralizing adaptive immune response, without the development of symptoms (St John et al., 2013a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: FcγRIII is the only activating Fc receptor that has been identified on mouse mast cells.
source: Each animal model of DENV has caveats, and in this case, it is important to emphasize that FcγRIII is the only activating Fc receptor that has been identified on mouse MCs.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about mouse mast cell biology.

claim: Human mast cells also express FcγRI as a second activating Fc receptor for IgG.
source: Human MCs also express FcγRI as a second activating Fc receptor for IgG (Malbec and Daëron, 2007), and the potential exists that both could mediate antibody-enhanced MC degranulation responses to DENV in humans.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Both FcγRI and FcγRIII could potentially mediate antibody-enhanced mast cell degranulation responses to DENV in humans.
source: Human MCs also express FcγRI as a second activating Fc receptor for IgG (Malbec and Daëron, 2007), and the potential exists that both could mediate antibody-enhanced MC degranulation responses to DENV in humans.
evidence: This is speculation based on the known expression of these receptors on human mast cells.

claim: The WT mouse model sustains replicating viral infection with the clinical isolate used in this study, particularly in lymphoid organs such as the spleen, and is also detectable in the liver.
source: Additionally, we have previously published that the WT mouse model sustains replicating viral infection with the clinical isolate used in this study, particularly in lymphoid organs such as the spleen, and is also detectable in the liver (St John et al., 2013b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The WT mouse model displays increased vascular leakage after heterologous challenge but does not show severe symptoms of frank hemorrhage or multi-organ failure characteristic of the most severe DENV infections.
source: Additionally, this WT mouse model displays increased vascular leakage after heterologous challenge; however, we have not observed the severe symptoms of frank hemorrhage or multi-organ failure that are characteristic of the approximately 1% of most severe DENV infections that are diagnosed as DHF/DSS.
evidence: This is a description of the limitations of the mouse model used in the study.

claim: Both anaphylaxis and DENV infection can ultimately result in systemic dysregulation of the vascular system, shock, and multiple organ dysfunction.
source: Certainly, the kinetics of viral infection is different from that of acute allergic responses involving vascular dysregulation. During infection, one would expect that ramping of antigen (in this case, virus) concentration in vivo would occur as infection spreads, in contrast to classical allergic responses, which are usually directed towards a bolus dose of exogenously derived antigen, such as food, drugs, or environmental substances.
evidence: This is presented as general knowledge about these two conditions.
